candidate.answerReason: Exact bounds show that more than one tenth of the original value remains after 21 years and less than one tenth remains after 22 years. The remaining value decreases each year, so 22 is the smallest qualifying integer.

methods.label: Bound the remaining value at consecutive years
methods.explanation:
Each year the money retains \(90\%\) of its previous value. Measured as a fraction of its original value, the amount remaining after \(n\) years is
\[
v_n=\left(\frac9{10}\right)^n.
\]
Losing at least \(90\%\) means \(v_n\le1/10\). To find the first qualifying year, we can compare the remaining values at consecutive years using exact bounds.

Squaring \((0.9)^5=0.59049\) gives
\[
\frac13<(0.9)^{10}=0.3486784401<\frac7{20}.
\]
The lower bound shows that after \(21\) years,
\[
(0.9)^{21}
=\frac9{10}\bigl((0.9)^{10}\bigr)^2
>\frac9{10}\left(\frac13\right)^2
=\frac1{10}.
\]
The upper bound shows that after \(22\) years,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(0.9)^{22}
&=\frac{81}{100}\bigl((0.9)^{10}\bigr)^2\\
&<\frac{81}{100}\left(\frac7{20}\right)^2
=\frac{3969}{40000}
<\frac1{10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining value decreases every year because it is multiplied by \(9/10\). Thus every year through \(21\) fails the requirement, while year \(22\) satisfies it. The smallest integer is \(22\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
